quotes.text: You think your system prompt is the law. The model thinks it's a suggestion, and the moment you ground it on internal content, one spicy document or user message can rewrite the rules mid-conversation.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Vividly explains why system prompts alone cannot stop prompt injection.

quotes.text: Prompt injection is that unsupervised intern who sounds helpful, writes in complete sentences, and then emails payroll data to their personal archive for safekeeping.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Captures the core argument for one identity per agent.

quotes.text: If you can't tell model output from tool output in your logs you're already in trouble

quotes.text: Why this matters? When injection wins, your agent becomes a data leaking poet. It hallucinates authority, escalates tools, and ignores policy language like it's the Wi-Fi terms of service.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

chapters.title: The one governance step most orgs skip

takeaways: Defend against prompt injection in code with tool allow lists, enforced JSON schema outputs, secret filters and fail-closed handling rather than relying on system prompts.
Give every agent its own service principal with scoped, time-bound roles and environment-separated connectors instead of shared credentials or tenant-wide scopes.
Make agent behavior provable with structured logs and end-to-end correlation IDs, enforce DLP on outputs, and gate releases with a repeatable red teaming checklist.
hook: AI agents in LangChain4j and Copilot Studio often ship with tenant-wide access, editable prompts and no audit trail. This episode walks architects and governance teams through three real failure cases and the fixes that hold: per-agent identities, an RBAC model, output DLP and a red teaming checklist.
